sections.summary: The neutral reading finds Paul completing the paidagogos argument with a household metaphor in which the minor heir is owner of the estate throughout his minority, his majority arrives on a date the father fixed in advance, and the Son and the Spirit are sent so that those under law receive adoption as sons and the standing of heir.
sections.relevance: Two features of the reading bear on permanence. First, the metaphor is built so that ownership is never in question: the minor 'differs in nothing from a slave' in daily experience yet is 'lord of all' the whole time, and the end of the minority is 'a date, not an achievement' fixed by the father rather than earned by the boy's conduct. Second, huiothesia is a formal legal act the reading describes as extinguishing prior liabilities, conferring inheritance rights identical to a natural son's, and being 'in principle irrevocable'; the Spirit's Abba cry is then the consequence and evidence of a sonship already held, not the mechanism producing it. The qualification is that the passage is arguing how the standing is constituted and by whom, against a proselyte procedure, not whether an established standing can later be forfeited.
key_phrases: though he is owner of everything
until the date set by the father
so that we might receive the adoption as sons
because you are sons, God sent forth the Spirit of his Son into our hearts
you are no longer a slave, but a son; and if a son, then an heir through God

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds Paul applying the coming-of-age figure to the Galatians' present course, reminding former idolaters that they have come to be known by God and asking how they can be turning back all over again to the weak and beggarly elements, closing with the fear that his labour over them has been for nothing.
sections.relevance: The paragraph puts the readers' movement in the opposite direction from 4:7: one verse after telling a man he is 'no longer a slave,' Paul asks how he can want to be enslaved 'again, over from the start,' with palin anothen doubled by design. The reading notes that eike ('in vain') is the word of 3:4, where Paul raised the possibility and immediately withdrew it, and that here he states it as a fear and does not withdraw it — so the outcome of his work among them is presented as genuinely open. Against a straightforward standing-loss reading, the same section relocates the initiative to God ('or rather to be known by God'), and the reading's own summary of the paragraph's force is that submitting to an externally imposed schedule as the condition of one's standing 'puts a person back in the posture of a minor' — a regression in posture, which is not the same as an assertion that sonship has been forfeited.
key_phrases: or rather to be known by God
how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements
to which you want to be enslaved all over again
I am afraid for you, that perhaps I have labored over you in vain

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds nine verses of personal appeal rather than argument — Paul recalling how the Galatians received him in illness, asking whether truth-telling has made him their enemy, exposing the rival teachers' motive in courting them, and describing himself as again in labour until Christ is formed in them.
sections.relevance: Only 4:19-20 touches the question, and it cuts both ways. Paul describes himself as in labour a second time over people he has already borne and says he is at a loss about them, which presents the outcome for these congregations as unsettled — consistent with the fear stated at 4:11. But the reading is explicit that what he says his labour is for is formation, not status: 'Not until you are properly admitted. Not until your status is secure... Until Christ takes shape in you.' On that account the section declines the question of standing rather than answering it, which is why the bearing here is weak.
key_phrases: for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you
they want to shut you out

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds Paul announcing an allegory and building two columns from Genesis — Hagar with Sinai and the present Jerusalem in slavery under Rome, Sarah with the Jerusalem above — quoting Isaiah 54:1 and then Genesis 21:10 in modified form, and concluding that 'we' are children of the free woman.
sections.relevance: The disinheritance language of 4:30 is conventionally pressed by the conditional-security side as showing that those who take up the wrong basis for standing are cast out and forfeit the inheritance. The neutral reading points elsewhere on three grounds. The columns are corporate and covenantal, not individual: what stands in Hagar's column is 'the present Jerusalem,' a temporal and political designation for a city under Roman rule, and a covenant named by what it produces when used this way — while Paul, a Jew by birth, places himself in the free column at 4:26 and 4:31, which limits what the allegory can be made to mean. The imperative 'cast out' must have a referent the Galatians can act on, and 4:29 has just identified a party operating among them now, so the letter's harshest sentence falls on the circumcision faction rather than on wavering members. And the reading stresses that the quoted words are Sarah's rather than God's, that Paul removed 'my son Isaac' from the citation to make it speak in his own terms, and that Genesis itself provides for the expelled son twice in the same chapter. What the section does affirm about the readers is an identity given by promise rather than by human contrivance — 'you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise' — which is a statement of how the standing arose, not of whether it can be lost.
key_phrases: she corresponds to the present Jerusalem
you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise
Cast out the slave woman and her son
the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman
we are not children of the slave woman but of the free
